about.title: Solving Quadratics by Factoring
about.length_note: About 30 minutes fits this class. It teaches one idea at a time: the zero product property, setting equal to zero, solving, then x-intercepts. Only one of my web searches returned results. The sources below back the link between zeros, factors and x-intercepts. The zero product property itself is standard algebra, but I have no textbook source for it, so those beats carry no citation.

sources.title: CCSS.Math.Content.HSA-APR.B.3: Identify zeros of polynomials when suitable factorizations are available, and use the zeros to construct a rough graph

sources.title: Graphing polynomials (Algebra blueprint, Graphing from Factors tasks)

say.text: Welcome to class 42. Today we solve quadratic equations by factoring. You already know how to factor from classes 36 to 39, so this is where it pays off.

show.text: Solving Quadratics by Factoring

say.text: First, what are we solving? A quadratic equation has an x² term in it. For example: x² + 5x + 6 = 0.

show.text: Quadratic equation: an equation with an x² term, like x² + 5x + 6 = 0

say.text: Our goal is to find every x that makes the equation true. Those values are called solutions. To get there, we need one small fact about zero.

show.text: Solution: a value of x that makes the equation true

say.text: Here it is. If two numbers multiply to make 0, then at least one of them has to be 0. That is the zero product property.

show.text: Zero product property: if a × b = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0 (or both)

say.text: See it with numbers. 0 × 7 is 0, and 5 × 0 is 0. But 3 × 4 is 12, and neither factor is zero. Only zero makes a product zero.

show.text: Product is 0: 0 × 7 = 0 and 5 × 0 = 0 | Product is not 0: 3 × 4 = 12 (no zero factor)

ask.q: You know a × b = 0, and a = 4. What must b be?
ask.why: 4 is not zero, so the zero has to come from b. Only zero times anything gives 0.

say.text: This only works when the product equals ZERO. If (x − 2)(x + 5) = 10, we can't say either factor is 10 or 0. We know nothing yet.

show.text: Works: (x − 2)(x + 5) = 0 | Does not work: (x − 2)(x + 5) = 10

ask.q: On which equation can you use the zero product property right away?
ask.why: The property needs a product that equals 0. The other equations have products equal to other numbers, so it says nothing about them.

say.text: So step one is to get zero on one side. Add or subtract terms until one side is 0. For x² + 3x = 10, subtract 10 from both sides.

show.text: x² + 3x = 10 | subtract 10 from both sides | x² + 3x − 10 = 0

ask.q: Which is x² − 4x = 12 rewritten with zero on one side?
ask.why: Subtract 12 from both sides. The −4x stays as it is, and the 12 becomes −12 on the left.

say.text: Step two is to factor the side that isn't zero. Our first example is x² + 5x + 6 = 0. We need two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5. Those are 2 and 3.
Step three is to set each factor equal to zero. Now the zero product property applies: either x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0.
Step four is to solve each little equation. x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2. x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3. Two solutions.

show.text: x = −2 or x = −3

say.text: Always check. Put −2 into the original: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0. It works. Put −3 in: 9 − 15 + 6 = 0. That works too.
Your turn. Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0. It's already zero on one side, so factor first, then set each factor to zero.

show.text: Try it: x² − 7x + 12 = 0

ask.q: What are the solutions of x² − 7x + 12 = 0?
ask.why: It factors as (x − 3)(x − 4) = 0. Then x − 3 = 0 gives x = 3 and x − 4 = 0 gives x = 4. The signs flip, because the factor is x − 3, not x + 3.

say.text: Quick vocabulary. The solutions of an equation like this are also called roots. If we write it as f(x) = 0, the same numbers are called zeros of the function. Three names, same numbers.

show.text: Solutions = roots = zeros (the x values that make the expression equal 0)

say.text: The Common Core standard for this uses the word zeros. It says to find zeros from a factorization, then use them to sketch a graph. That is where we go next.

show.text: Find zeros when a factorization is available, then use them for a rough graph (paraphrase of standard A-APR.B.3)

say.text: Here's the picture link. If a is a zero, then the point (a, 0) is on the graph. So the graph touches the x-axis at x = a. Zeros are x-intercepts.

show.text: A U-shaped parabola opening upward. It crosses the horizontal x-axis at two points, x = −3 and x = −2, and dips below the axis between them.

say.text: So when we solved x² + 5x + 6 = 0, we also found where the graph of y = x² + 5x + 6 crosses the x-axis: at −3 and −2. Factored form shows the intercepts.

show.text: Equation: x² + 5x + 6 = 0 gives x = −2, −3 | Graph: y = x² + 5x + 6 crosses the x-axis at (−2, 0) and (−3, 0)

ask.q: A parabola crosses the x-axis at x = 1 and x = 5. What are the solutions of the equation where y = 0?
ask.why: Where y = 0 is exactly where the graph meets the x-axis. So the x-intercepts are the solutions.

say.text: Next, a trap. Try x² − 9x = 0. There's no constant term, but we can still factor out a common x: x(x − 9) = 0.
Don't divide both sides by x. You'd lose the solution x = 0. Factor instead, and both solutions show up.

show.text: Factor out x. Don't divide by x. Dividing loses a solution.

ask.q: What are the solutions of x² + 4x = 0?
ask.why: Factor x(x + 4) = 0. Then x = 0, or x + 4 = 0 gives x = −4. The 0 is a real solution, so keep it.

say.text: The same steps work when the x² has a number in front. Solve 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0. It factors as (2x − 1)(x + 3) = 0. You can check by multiplying it back out.
Now solve each piece. 2x − 1 = 0 means 2x = 1, so x = 1/2. And x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3. Solutions can be fractions, and that's fine.

ask.q: In (3x + 6)(x − 2) = 0, what does the factor 3x + 6 = 0 give?
ask.why: Subtract 6 to get 3x = −6, then divide by 3 to get x = −2. You have to do both steps to isolate x.

say.text: Now a game-style problem. A ball is kicked up, and its height in meters after t seconds is h = −5t² + 20t. These numbers are made up to keep the math clean. When is the height 0?
The two zeros tell a story. At t = 0 the ball is on the ground, about to leave. At t = 4 it's back on the ground. Both are x-intercepts of the path.

show.text: An upside-down U-shaped arc. It starts on the ground at 0 seconds, peaks at 2 seconds, and lands at 4 seconds.

ask.q: Using h = −5t² + 20t, when does the ball land?
ask.why: The ball is at height 0 at t = 0 (the start) and t = 4 (the landing). The later time is the landing.

say.text: Let's put it all together. Four steps: zero on one side, factor, set each factor to zero, solve each. Then check, and connect the answers to the x-intercepts.

show.text: 1. Get 0 on one side | 2. Factor | 3. Set each factor = 0 | 4. Solve each | Check, then link to x-intercepts

say.text: Watch for three slips. Using the property when the product isn't zero. Dividing by x and losing a solution. Forgetting that (x − 3) gives x = +3. Nice work today. Next class is square roots and completing the square.

show.text: Slip 1: product not 0 | Slip 2: dividing by x | Slip 3: sign flip, (x − 3) gives x = 3

other_side.claim: Factoring is the best first way to solve a quadratic.
other_side.other_view: Factoring only works neatly when the numbers factor nicely. Many quadratics don't, so completing the square and the quadratic formula (classes 43 and 44) work on every quadratic. A calculator can also graph it and read the x-intercepts. Factoring is quick and shows the structure, but it is one tool among several. This is a teaching-order note from the course plan, not from a source I read.
